title: Chapter VII: Transition from a College to a Public School
text:
Chapter VII

Transition from a College to a Public School

THE BURNING OF THE COLLEGE PLANT

Savoy College came to an abrupt and untimely end with the burning of its plant on the night of July 3, 1890. The destruction was complete. Savoy had no fire department, and bucket-brigade methods were ineffectual to combat the flames in the close group of wooden buildings. Ex-students who lived in Savoy remember vividly the scene as faculty members and citizens strove to save the town's chief enterprise and claim to distinction and finally had to stand back out of range of explosions as the flames reached the chemistry laboratory and burst out in varicolored displays of fireworks. The library smoldered until the break of day.

PLANS FOR REBUILDING

The restoration of the plant was obviously beyond the financial abilities of the faculty members who owned it, but an effort was made to re-establish an equivalent preparatory school on some basis. A news story in The Dallas Morning News a few days after the fire reported the situation optimistically:

Savoy, Fannin County, Texas, July 10.—The citizens of this place have held several meetings for the purpose of building a college since the burning of the old one on the night of the 3rd. They met last night and raised $4,000 in subscriptions. They are building on the old foundations. The school has 200 or more pupils and will have it completed so as to be ready for the term commencing September 1. The town will doubtless have a boom they have never before witnessed, and property has already advanced in price from 20 to 25 per cent. The surrounding country expects of a fine yield of both corn and cotton, but they are greatly needed since the fire.
